articles.summary: $1.6 Billion South Mississippi Natural Gas Pipeline Project Approved by Energy Transfer  Construction Review
articles.full_text:
Energy Transfer LP has formally committed to developing the $1.6 billion South Mississippi Pipeline, a major natural gas infrastructure project designed to transport up to 1.2 billion cubic feet of gas per day (Bcf/d) from Louisiana across Mississippi. The proposed 215-mile (346-kilometer) pipeline comes as demand for natural gas continues to increase across the United States. This is mainly from liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facilities and power generation infrastructure supporting the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence (AI) data center industry.
The project, which will be developed by Energy Transfer Interstate Holdings, is expected to strengthen natural gas transportation capacity across the southeastern United States. Energy Transfer plans to own a 51% stake in the pipeline and operate the system, while project customers are expected to hold the remaining 49%.
According to the project details, the South Mississippi Natural Gas Pipeline will start at a proposed receipt point in Richland Parish, Louisiana, and extend to a new delivery point in the George County area of Mississippi. The proposed infrastructure will also comprise 215 miles of either 42-inch or 36-inch-diameter pipeline, alongside associated compression and metering facilities.
Additionally, the pipeline is designed to provide additional firm natural gas transportation capacity. It will also improve access to supplies from multiple production basins across the southeastern United States.
Furthermore, Energy Transfer has secured binding commitments from anchor shippers. The company continues to seek additional customer commitments through a binding open season scheduled to close on November 25, 2026.
South Mississippi Pipeline Project Targets 2030 Completion
Energy Transfer expects the South Mississippi Natural Gas Pipeline to enter commercial service by March 1, 2030. The company is also expected to seek authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to construct the proposed facilities.
The pipeline’s development is expected to progress through additional customer commitments, project design and regulatory review before construction can proceed.
Energy Transfer has also indicated that it intends to co-locate most of the proposed expansion with existing infrastructure. This is intended to minimize impacts on landowners and surrounding communities while simplifying the regulatory review process.
Additionally, the final pipeline configuration and capacity will be influenced by the outcome of the open season and the transportation commitments secured from prospective customers.
AI Data Center Expansion Fuels Natural Gas Infrastructure Investment
The South Mississippi Pipeline Project also comes amid a broader expansion of natural gas infrastructure across the United States. This is as pipeline operators respond to increasing demand from electricity generation, industrial consumers and LNG export terminals.
In particular, the rapid development of AI infrastructure has created additional demand for reliable electricity supplies. It has also created demand for chip making facilities across the U.S. with others such as the Samsung semiconductor plant in Taylor, Texas looking toward large scale industrial expansion. Large data centers require substantial and continuous power. This has prompted utilities and independent power developers to consider new natural gas-fired generation capacity alongside renewable energy and other electricity sources.
Energy Transfer is among the infrastructure operators positioning its pipeline network to serve this emerging market. The company also previously disclosed long-term natural gas supply arrangements with Oracle for its US data center operations.
Beyond the South Mississippi gas project, Energy Transfer is advancing other pipeline and capacity expansion investments. This is in a bid to improve connectivity between natural gas production regions and major consumption markets.
Once completed, the South Mississippi Natural Gas Pipeline Project is expected to provide additional transportation capacity for natural gas supplies moving through the Gulf Coast and southeastern US markets. This is expected to support US Southeast’s expanding energy and industrial requirements.

articles.title: China Moves to Expand Control of Global Critical Minerals Through Overseas Mining Investments - Brand Icon Image
articles.summary: China Moves to Expand Control of Global Critical Minerals Through Overseas Mining Investments  Brand Icon Image
articles.full_text:
China is stepping up efforts to secure greater control of the global mining industry by mobilising state-linked companies to acquire larger stakes in overseas mineral assets, in a move aimed at strengthening its influence over resources essential to electric vehicles, semiconductors and jet engines.
The strategy is expected to give Beijing greater influence over global supplies of critical minerals and determine which countries and companies have access to them, according to analysts.
Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group, described the development as a shift towards a coordinated government-led approach to overseas mining investments.
“China is rolling out a state-coordinated global mining strategy” to replace firm-level decision-making, Wang said, adding that the approach would support larger investments that are better aligned with the country's strategic interests.
As part of the initiative, China established a dedicated overseas bureau in April to supervise foreign investments by centrally administered state-owned enterprises. Several government agencies, ministries and policy banks have also been brought into the process to guide and facilitate overseas mining transactions.
In July, the country further strengthened the arrangement with the establishment of a mining investment vehicle designed to coordinate foreign mining deals. The body is expected to advise Chinese companies on regulatory compliance, risk management and market conditions as they navigate increasing geopolitical tensions and regulatory restrictions in foreign markets.
According to Wang, the centralised approach could reduce unhealthy competition among Chinese companies while improving their ability to compete with Western investors and emerging players such as Saudi Arabia and India.
However, she warned that longer approval and review procedures could increase corruption risks and potentially reduce investment returns.
Chinese companies have spent the past two decades expanding their presence in overseas mining operations, making substantial investments in countries that Western mining firms have often overlooked, including Tajikistan and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The latest drive has become increasingly important as governments worldwide recognise critical minerals as strategic resources capable of influencing economic and geopolitical relationships.
Data from Rhodium Group showed that Chinese acquisitions of overseas mineral assets reached $8.8bn in the first three quarters of the year, representing the highest annual total since at least 2018.
Armand Meyer, senior research analyst at Rhodium Group, said the acquisitions had largely focused on minerals where China's domestic production was insufficient.
“Acquisitions have mostly been concentrated in minerals that China lacks domestically,” Meyer said, identifying lithium, nickel and cobalt as major targets during the electric vehicle expansion of the mid-2010s, while gold has attracted greater attention in recent years.
Beijing seeks to secure mineral supplies
China's growing interest in overseas mining is also driven by concerns about its dependence on foreign suppliers for essential raw materials.
According to Eurasia Group, outbound investments in upstream critical minerals are expected to roughly double compared with the 2021–2025 period as Beijing intensifies efforts to secure access to resources and reserves that are limited within its borders.
Wang said the Chinese government regarded dependence on imports of about 70 per cent as an implicit national security threshold.
This has placed minerals such as copper, lithium, cobalt, nickel, bauxite and iron ore under significant pressure for increased overseas sourcing and investment.
Even in areas where China's import dependence remains below that threshold, the government is seeking to expand its access to strategic resources.
Gold, for instance, remains within what Beijing considers a 50 per cent safe dependence range. Nevertheless, Wang said China was still pursuing greater access to high-grade gold deposits.
She noted that the country's determination to achieve scale and strengthen its geopolitical influence could sometimes take precedence over conventional considerations of investment risks and profitability.
Processing capacity creates fresh tensions
Despite China's aggressive expansion into overseas mining, its investment strategy is encountering resistance from resource-rich countries seeking to retain more economic value from their mineral resources.
Several host governments are increasingly demanding that foreign investors establish local processing and refining facilities rather than exporting minerals in their raw form.
The development presents a challenge for China, which has established a dominant position in mineral processing and refining, turning the sector into a major strategic advantage in global supply chains.
For years, countries have shipped rare earth minerals to China for processing because refining involves significant environmental costs and requires substantial industrial investment. This enabled Beijing to develop extensive processing infrastructure and strengthen its dominance in the sector.
The United States, despite possessing considerable rare earth resources, remains heavily dependent on China for refining.
According to the International Energy Agency, China accounts for approximately 92 per cent of global refined rare earth production.
Brad Handler, director of the Energy Finance Lab at the Payne Institute, said China's dominant position gives it considerable influence over global prices and supply availability.
He explained that Beijing could use its processing advantage to undermine competing investments by increasing production and flooding the market with cheaper materials.
“If a rival builds a new refinery, China can produce more, oversupply the market and push prices below economic levels,” Handler said.
Export restrictions raise concerns
China's control of rare earth processing has also become more significant following restrictions introduced on the export of seven medium and heavy rare earth elements since last year.
Under the measures, exporters are required to obtain government licences before shipping the affected materials overseas.
Japan has reportedly been among the countries most affected by the restrictions, with concerns that its supplies of yttrium could run out within months.
Yttrium is used in the production of display screens and semiconductors and is generally obtained as a by-product during the extraction of other rare earth elements.
Chinese customs data showed that China's exports of yttrium oxide to Japan fell sharply to 4,000 kilogrammes in September, compared with 51,000 kilogrammes recorded in the same month a year earlier.
The supply disruption has also driven up prices outside China. Reports indicated that yttrium oxide was selling for approximately $1,150 per kilogramme in overseas markets, about 179 times its price two years earlier, while the domestic price in China remained around $9 per kilogramme.
Japan previously spent 16 years building strategic stockpiles following China's export restrictions in 2010. However, Bedford noted that the country still faced significant challenges in developing alternative processing facilities.
“There is virtually no yttrium or lutetium separation capacity outside of China,” Bedford said.
Chinese firms shift investment strategy
Meanwhile, Chinese mining companies are adjusting their overseas investment strategies in response to growing regulatory pressure from host countries.
Rather than relying exclusively on outright acquisitions, companies have increasingly turned to greenfield investments, establishing new mining and processing facilities closer to mineral deposits, according to Rhodium Group.
Meyer said the approach was particularly evident in countries where governments had introduced policies requiring local processing before minerals could be exported.
He cited Indonesia's ban on nickel ore exports as an example, noting that the policy had encouraged Chinese companies to invest in smelting and refining facilities within the Southeast Asian country instead of shipping raw nickel ore to China.
The development reflects China's broader effort to maintain its influence over critical mineral supply chains while adapting to changing government policies and growing competition for strategic resources.
As countries increasingly seek greater control over their mineral wealth, China's expanding overseas investments are likely to remain a major factor in the global competition for resources essential to modern technology, manufacturing and national security.

articles.full_text:
Cabinet clears ₹2,814-crore support for lithium, nickel processing plants
The five-year scheme offers a 30 per cent capital subsidy for four lithium and nickel processing plants, aiming to reduce import dependence and strengthen critical mineral supply chains
Listen to This Article
The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a ₹2,814-crore capital expenditure support scheme to establish domestic critical mineral processing plants for lithium and nickel, a move welcomed by industry players who said it would address a key gap in India’s critical mineral value chain and help reduce dependence on imports of refined materials.
Under the scheme, which will run for five years from FY27 to FY31, the government will provide a capital subsidy of 30 per cent of eligible investment for setting up two lithium processing plants and two nickel processing plants. The plants will have minimum processing capacities of 30,000 tonnes each for lithium and 50,000 tonnes each for nickel.
The maximum capital support has been capped at ₹500 crore per beneficiary for lithium processing plants and ₹900 crore per beneficiary for nickel processing plants.
The scheme aims to develop domestic processing capabilities for converting lithium and nickel ores and intermediate products into high-purity compounds. Cobalt is also expected to be recovered as a by-product of nickel processing.
Beneficiaries will be selected through a two-stage process, beginning with technical qualification, followed by financial bidding. For each mineral, two beneficiaries will be selected based on the least-cost criterion, with preference given to bidders seeking the lowest capital expenditure support from the government. The incentives will be disbursed in three tranches linked to the achievement of specified milestones.
Also Read
The scheme comes against the backdrop of India's substantial dependence on imports of refined intermediates and high-purity materials, including lithium, nickel and cobalt. The government said domestic beneficiation and processing infrastructure for these minerals remains at a nascent stage, with commercial-scale projects facing challenges such as high capital requirements, limited availability of suitable technologies and constrained access to raw materials.
At an industry event last month, Union Mines Secretary Keshav Chandra said the government was working to establish critical mineral processing parks in four states — Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.
"All these four parks will have their own ecosystem for a particular mineral," Chandra said, adding that the parks in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh would focus on rare earth elements, while those in Maharashtra and Odisha would cater to lithium and nickel, respectively.
Attero co-founder and CEO Nitin Gupta said the scheme addressed a key gap in India's critical mineral value chain — domestic processing capacity. While the country was taking steps to secure access to critical mineral resources, developing the ability to process them into high-purity materials was equally important to reduce import dependence and strengthen supply chain security, he said.
LOHUM founder and CEO Rajat Verma said the scheme could help India move from importing refined materials towards developing domestic supplies by supporting facilities that convert lithium and nickel into high-purity compounds.
"As a processor of both, LOHUM welcomes this decisive step," he said.
The scheme complements the government's existing support for critical mineral recycling, creating incentives for both the processing of primary mineral resources and the recovery of metals from used batteries and electronic waste, said Rajesh Gupta, managing director and founder of Evergreen Recyclekaro India.
"Together, these initiatives can help build a more dependable domestic supply chain for critical minerals," he said, adding that lithium, nickel and cobalt compounds also have applications in chemicals, catalysts, pharmaceuticals, speciality steel and defence.
The proposed facilities are expected to support sectors such as electric mobility, battery energy storage systems, electronics, defence and speciality steel, while strengthening domestic value addition and reducing reliance on overseas processing capacities.

articles.full_text:
New Delhi: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing with a total financial outlay of ₹2,814 crore over five years. The scheme aims to strengthen India’s domestic critical mineral processing capabilities, reduce dependence on imports and develop a resilient supply chain for minerals such as lithium and nickel.
The scheme will be implemented during the financial years 2026-27 to 2030-31 and will provide targeted capital expenditure support for establishing and operationalising domestic critical mineral processing facilities.
The initiative is expected to promote value addition within the country and strengthen India’s position across the critical mineral value chain. It will also support key sectors, including electric mobility, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), electronics, defence and speciality steel.
Why Has the Government Approved the Critical Mineral Processing Scheme?
The processing of critical minerals is currently concentrated in a limited number of countries, making global supply chains vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions, price volatility and potential supply restrictions. These challenges pose risks to India’s economic security, national security and long-term industrial development. They may also affect the country’s efforts to achieve its decarbonisation targets.
India continues to depend substantially on imports for refined intermediates and high-purity materials because its domestic beneficiation and critical mineral processing infrastructure is still at an early stage of development.
Domestic processing capacity for minerals such as lithium, nickel and cobalt remains limited. Commercial-scale projects also face several challenges, including high capital investment requirements, limited access to suitable technologies and constraints in the availability of raw materials.
Against this backdrop, the government has introduced the scheme to encourage investment in domestic processing infrastructure, promote import substitution and establish resilient end-to-end critical mineral value chains.

₹2,814 Crore Outlay for Lithium and Nickel Processing Plants
The scheme has a total financial outlay of ₹2,814 crore and will remain operational from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31.
Under the initiative, the government will provide a capital subsidy of 30% of eligible investment for establishing four critical mineral processing plants.
These facilities will include:
- Two Lithium Processing Plants: Each plant will have a minimum processing capacity of 30 kilotonnes (kt).
- Two Nickel Processing Plants: Each plant will have a minimum processing capacity of 50 kilotonnes (kt).
The scheme is designed to support the processing of lithium and nickel ores and intermediary products into high-purity compounds. Cobalt is also expected to be recovered as a by-product of nickel production.
Capital Subsidy and Financial Support Under the Scheme
To encourage investment in domestic processing facilities, the government has set separate maximum capital support limits for lithium and nickel processing projects.
The financial assistance will be provided as follows:
- Lithium Processing: Maximum capital support of ₹500 crore per beneficiary.
- Nickel Processing: Maximum capital support of ₹900 crore per beneficiary.
- Capital Subsidy: 30% of the eligible investment.
The financial support is intended to reduce the initial investment burden on companies and encourage the establishment of commercial-scale processing facilities in India.
How Will Beneficiaries Be Selected?
The government will follow a two-stage selection process to identify beneficiaries under the Critical Mineral Processing Scheme.
In the first stage, applications will be evaluated for technical qualifications. Only applicants meeting the prescribed technical criteria will be eligible to participate in the second stage. The second stage will involve financial bidding. For each mineral, two beneficiaries will be selected based on the least-cost criterion. This means applicants seeking the lowest capital expenditure support from the government will be given preference.
The incentives will be disbursed in three tranches, linked to the achievement of specified milestones under the scheme.
Scheme to Strengthen India’s Critical Mineral Value Chain
The scheme is expected to strengthen domestic capabilities in processing critical minerals and reduce India’s dependence on overseas suppliers for high-purity materials. The development of domestic lithium and nickel processing facilities will support industries that rely on these minerals, particularly electric mobility, battery manufacturing, energy storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
By encouraging private investment and promoting domestic value addition, the initiative is expected to improve supply chain resilience and create a stronger industrial ecosystem for critical minerals.
Boost to Atmanirbhar Bharat Initiative
The approval of the ₹2,814 crore Capex Support Scheme marks an important step towards advancing the objectives of Atmanirbhar Bharat.
By supporting domestic processing infrastructure, the government aims to strengthen India’s economic and strategic security, promote import substitution and develop a reliable critical mineral supply chain.
The initiative will also help build domestic capabilities across the critical mineral value chain, supporting India’s long-term industrial growth and clean energy transition.

articles.title: Critical minerals are more than mining - Metal Tech News
articles.summary: Critical minerals are more than mining  Metal Tech News

Metal Tech News - November 3, 2026
As efforts around strengthening our domestic critical-mineral supply chains evolve, it is more important than ever that the U.S. adopts a strategy that doesn't stop at what comes out of the ground: the U.S. also needs processing and manufacturing capabilities to turn those materials into products here at home.
Oklahoma might be the best example of how states with the resources, infrastructure, and workforce to support these activities can contribute to that broader effort.
The critical minerals our nation's largest businesses rely on, including lithium, aluminum, and graphite, require extensive refining processes to break them down into their most basic chemical forms before they can be reconfigured into products such as semiconductor chips or batteries.
Historically, the United States has relied on partnerships with foreign countries, including China, to process raw materials into components that can then be turned into final products. However, as tensions around foreign trade escalate, it is essential to strengthen the capacity to process and refine these minerals here at home.
Oklahoma provides a case study in how advanced manufacturing and mineral processing can strengthen the domestic supply chain. Investments from USA Rare Earth and Stardust Power, among others, demonstrate how different parts of the critical-minerals and advanced-manufacturing ecosystem can develop within the same state.
USA Rare Earth operates a rare-earth magnet manufacturing facility in Stillwater, Oklahoma, to produce magnets used in electric vehicles, defense systems, semiconductors, and other advanced technologies.
As for Stardust Power, the company is developing a central lithium processing facility in Muskogee, Oklahoma, with the anticipated capacity of up to 50,000 metric tons per annum of battery-grade lithium carbonate for the battery and energy-storage supply chains.
These projects are supported by the state's existing energy resources, infrastructure, workforce, and industrial base, creating conditions for companies not only to start but expand operations in the United States.
While they are not intended to replace crucial international supply chains, they can help strengthen the domestic capabilities that support them.
A domestic supply chain isn't a single facility or stage of production. It's an integral part of a larger ecosystem in which each part needs the others to function, and extraction from the mine is only the beginning.
When critical minerals are first pulled from the ground, they are found in a state of ore concentrate and are mixed with other rock and minerals. For rare earth minerals to become usable to manufacturers, they must be refined to meet purity standards and broken down into their individual chemical compounds to isolate the targeted mineral.
This requires manufacturers and processors that are capable of turning those refined minerals and compounds into usable components or products, making solid infrastructure behind these processes just as important as mining for the critical minerals.
Processing and manufacturing facilities also require reliable access to energy, water, and transportation corridors. With Oklahoma's industrial energy rates 20%-40% below the national average and over 400 miles of waterways connecting Oklahoma to the Mississippi River and the Gulf of Mexico, the state is primed to provide affordable energy for these projects as well as a sturdy logistical supply chain to move minerals.
However, there would be no processes to support and uphold without the base of a strong workforce.
Critical mineral processing and advanced manufacturing require employees with experience in areas such as chemical processing, engineering, equipment operation, and industrial maintenance. As more companies invest in these capabilities, developing a workforce with the technical skills to support increasingly specialized operations will be important to maintaining growth.
A company processing one critical mineral may create demand for nearby manufacturers, suppliers, or recycling operations, while existing industrial infrastructure and workforce capabilities can make a region more attractive to companies considering new investments. Over time, these connections can help create a more complete domestic ecosystem rather than a collection of individual projects.
Building a stronger domestic critical minerals supply chain will also require significant investment, and those investments must ultimately make economic sense for the companies and states involved.
Separation and refining of the materials represent a major share of total mine-to-product costs, as rare earths contain multiple elements that must be separated through highly complicated processes. Mining, crushing, milling, and chemical processing of these materials can also be energy- and water-intensive, adding higher operating and capital costs.
Rare earth projects also often face a "financing gap," as developers must invest heavily in exploration, technology, and facilities before proving their performance. That means customers may hesitate to commit to long-term purchases until production has been demonstrated.
Strengthening domestic capacity does not mean the United States should view it as a replacement for international trade. Different countries have access to different mineral resources, technologies, and manufacturing capabilities, and the United States will continue to benefit from those relationships.
Attempting to develop every stage of every critical mineral supply chain entirely within the United States would be costly and, in many cases, unrealistic.
The goal should instead be greater resilience. By developing more processing, refining, and manufacturing capabilities at home, the United States can reduce its dependence on a limited number of foreign sources and have greater flexibility when disruptions affect global supply chains.
Domestic capacity also provides another option when international markets become more difficult to navigate, while maintaining relationships with international trading partners allows American companies to continue benefiting from resources and capabilities that are not available domestically.
That broader approach is already taking shape in places such as Oklahoma, where investments across different stages of the mineral supply chain offer one example of how domestic capacity can develop.
The state is working to become the next big hub for aluminum through the proposed aluminum smelter in Inola, Okla., which is estimated to bring $49 billion in cumulative economic impact through 2060 and includes more than 1,000 permanent direct jobs and 4,000-plus construction jobs.
The opportunity is not simply to produce more minerals, but to strengthen the connections between the resources, infrastructure, workforce, and industries needed to turn those materials into finished products.

articles.title: China accelerates overseas mining investment to secure critical minerals - Mining.com.au
articles.summary: China accelerates overseas mining investment to secure critical minerals  Mining.com.au
articles.full_text:
China is stepping up its acquisitions of overseas mining assets to strengthen its control over global mineral supply chains, with analysts expecting investment to accelerate in the coming years.
According to CNBC, Chinese state-owned companies have invested heavily in overseas mining over the past two decades, often targeting regions overlooked by Western miners.
That push has gained urgency as governments increasingly view critical minerals as a source of geopolitical leverage, while countries such as Saudi Arabia and India emerge as competing investors.
A report by Rhodium Group cited by CNBC estimates that Chinese overseas mineral acquisitions reached US$8.8 billion ($12.52 billion) in the first nine months of 2026 – already the highest annual total since at least 2018.
“Acquisitions have mostly been concentrated in minerals that China lacks domestically,” Armand Meyer, senior research analyst at Rhodium Group, says.
These have included lithium, nickel, and cobalt during the electric vehicle boom in the mid-2010s, followed by growing interest in gold in recent years.
Australian think tank Climate Energy Finance previously estimated that China has invested over US$120 billion in overseas mining ventures since 2023.
Beijing steps up investment strategy
Analysts at Eurasia Group expect China’s overseas mining investments to increase significantly as Beijing seeks to secure long-term access to strategic mineral reserves.
The consultancy estimates that Chinese outbound investment in upstream critical minerals could double compared with levels recorded during the 2021–2025 period.
Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group, says the spending forms part of a ‘state-coordinated’ global mining strategy to allow for large mining investments.
As part of that strategy, Beijing established a dedicated overseas bureau in April to oversee foreign investments by central state-owned enterprises.
It also created a mining investment vehicle in July to coordinate overseas deals and advise Chinese companies on compliance, risk management, and market conditions.
According to Wang, Beijing treats 70% import dependence as an implicit red line, placing minerals such as copper, lithium, cobalt, nickel, bauxite, and iron ore under greater pressure to secure overseas supplies.
Even for minerals where import reliance is lower, China is looking to expand its access to resources, she adds.
Gold, for example, falls within what Wang describes as a relatively safe import dependence range of 50%, but Beijing is still seeking access to more high-grade deposits.
Growing resistance to China’s dominance
However, this overseas investment spree is facing resistance from local refiners seeking to capture more value from their minerals instead of relying on Chinese processing.
For decades, resource-rich countries have shipped raw minerals such as rare earths to China for processing, partly because refining can carry significant environmental costs.
This has allowed China to build extensive processing capacity, giving it a dominant position in the global rare earth market.
According to the International Energy Agency, China accounts for approximately 92% of global refined rare earth production.
Brad Handler, director of the Energy Finance Lab at the Payne Institute, says this dominance gives Beijing the ability to influence global prices by restricting supply or increasing production.
“If a rival builds a new refinery, China can produce more, oversupply the market, and push prices below economic levels,” Handler says.
China has also tightened its control over rare earth exports, introducing licensing requirements for seven medium and heavy rare earth elements last year.
The restrictions have affected overseas buyers, including Japan, where supplies of key minerals like yttrium are running short, as Mining.com.au reported last month.

Cabinet approves five-year ₹2,814 cr push for critical mineral processing
The five-year scheme aims to strengthen India's critical mineral ecosystem, with implementation scheduled from 2026-27 to 2030-31
Listen to This Article
The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a ₹2,814-crore capital expenditure support scheme to promote domestic processing of critical minerals, targeting the setting up of four plants for lithium and nickel, Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said.
The scheme, which will run for five years from FY27 to FY31, will provide a capital subsidy of 30 per cent of eligible investment for setting up two lithium processing plants and two nickel processing plants.
The two lithium plants will have a minimum processing capacity of 30,000 tonnes each, while the two nickel plants will have a minimum capacity of 50,000 tonnes each. The maximum capital support will be capped at ₹500 crore per lithium beneficiary and ₹900 crore per nickel beneficiary, according to a statement issued by the Cabinet.
The scheme aims to establish domestic processing facilities to convert lithium and nickel ores and intermediary products into high-purity compounds. Cobalt is also expected to be recovered as a by-product of nickel production.
The facilities are expected to support critical sectors such as electric mobility, battery energy storage systems (BESS), electronics, defence and speciality steel.
Also Read
In the statement, the Cabinet noted that the processing of critical minerals remains geographically concentrated in a "few global locations", exposing supply chains to geopolitical disruptions, price volatility and potential supply restrictions. This poses risks to supply chain resilience and economic security, the Cabinet noted.
India remains substantially dependent on imports for refined intermediates and high-purity materials because domestic beneficiation and processing infrastructure for critical minerals, including lithium, nickel and cobalt, is still at a nascent stage. 
According to NITI Aayog's September 2026 Trade Watch report, India is 100 per cent import-dependent for lithium, nickel and cobalt. China accounted for 26.2 per cent of India's nickel imports in 2025, 52.3 per cent of synthetic graphite imports, 22.6 per cent of lithium oxide and hydroxide imports and 34.3 per cent of lithium carbonate imports. 
China's dominance is even more pronounced globally. The International Energy Agency (IEA), in its Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2025, estimated that China accounted for 70-75 per cent of global lithium and cobalt processing and more than 90 per cent of rare earth and battery-grade graphite refining.
The Cabinet said domestic processing capacity remained limited, with commercial-scale projects facing challenges such as high capital requirements, limited availability of suitable technologies and constrained access to raw materials. Building domestic capacity is therefore important for increasing value addition within the country, reducing import dependence and establishing resilient end-to-end value chains.
Beneficiaries under the scheme will be selected through a two-stage process. Applications will first be assessed for technical qualification, with only eligible applicants allowed to participate in the subsequent financial bidding process.
For each mineral, two beneficiaries will be selected on the basis of the least-cost criterion, meaning those seeking the lowest capital expenditure support from the government. The incentives will be disbursed in three tranches linked to the achievement of specified milestones.

Industrial certification provider Isometric announced today the launch of Ready for CBAM, a new service aimed at helping companies exporting to the EU prepare emissions data for verification under the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the EU’s carbon tax on imported goods.
CBAM was adopted in 2023, and entered into force at the beginning of 2026, to establish a mechanism designed to avoid “carbon leakage,” a situation in which companies move production of emissions-intensive goods to countries with less stringent environmental and climate policies. CBAM is aimed at equalizing the price of carbon paid for EU products operating under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) – the EU’s internal cap and trade carbon pricing mechanism – with that paid for products produced in other countries, with companies that import into the EU required to purchase CBAM certificates in order to make up the difference.
Under CBAM, EU importers are required to purchase certificates covering the emissions embedded in imported goods, calculated using either actual emissions data verified by an accredited verifier or default values established by the EU. For most covered goods, the default values include a markup that increases from 10% in 2026 to 30% by 2028, potentially increasing costs for importers without verified emissions data.
EU importers are required to submit their first CBAM declarations, covering 2026 imports, by September 30, 2027. Errors in submissions may require additional rounds of review, Isometric said.
Under the new service, Isometric said that its carbon accounting experts work with exporters to prepare the monitoring plan and emissions report for each plant, with its AI-powered platform checking the data as it is uploaded and flagging any issues, while the experts then review the full submission against the EU’s rules. The service continues through the verification process, with the experts working with the exporter to resolve issues raised by the verifier, Isometric added.
The company said that the new service covers all six current sectors under CBAM, including cement, iron and steel, aluminum, fertilizers, hydrogen, and electricity.
Lukas May, Chief Commercial Officer, Isometric, said:
“Exporters are going into their first CBAM verification with very little guidance on what a good submission looks like, and no way of knowing how long the process will take. The best way to avoid repeating it is to get the monitoring plan and emissions report right before they reach the verifier.”
The launch of the new service follows Isometric’s Series A financing round, with the company raising $50 million, as it moves to extend its AI-powered certification platform from its initial focus on carbon markets to the broader industrial economy, including areas such as industrial emissions, energy, fuels, and materials.

articles.title: Critical Minerals Diplomacy: What over 200 agreements reveal - International Institute for Sustainable Development
articles.summary: Critical Minerals Diplomacy: What over 200 agreements reveal  International Institute for Sustainable Development
articles.full_text:
The last two years have brought a new priority to global economic diplomacy: critical minerals now feature in most trade and economic agreements. The rush to secure resources needed for the climate and digital transitions has pushed all large consumers to compete for availability and security of supply. The US is at the heart of the complicated web of bilateral agreements, yet an immense effort to get a share of this pie is being exerted by all the major players – such as the EU, Japan, China, and India – and some unexpected ones, such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE. IISD’s Trade and Climate Tracker provides insight on where to build on existing cooperation to better impact climate and communities.
Need to Know
- Critical minerals are now central to economic diplomacy: 139 of the 211 trade and economic agreements signed since January 2025 and mapped in the IISD's Trade & Climate Tracker are linked to critical raw materials.
- The United States leads by a wide margin, with 41 CRM-linked agreements largely driven by security and technology concerns. But India, China, Canada, Saudi Arabia, the EU, the UAE, and Japan are also signing deals at pace.
- Resource-rich countries are in demand, and they’re using these deals to push for local processing and stronger value chains at home. Some are also cooperating with each other.
- Most CRM deals (68%) are MoUs and other non-binding instruments. They are fast to agree but weaker on follow-through, and 39% of these texts are not made public.
- Climate is largely missing: only 1 of the 60 CRM-centred agreements include energy provisions, and none address climate governance.
- To make this moment count, future deals should share value with producing countries, link minerals cooperation to climate goals, and make their texts public.
From friction to cooperation
Demand for critical minerals is rising on several fronts. The energy transition requires lithium, cobalt, nickel and graphite for batteries; rare earths for wind turbines and electric vehicle motors; and copper for power grids. The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers is adding pressure on supplies of copper for power and cooling, gallium and germanium for chips, and rare earths for hardware. Defence needs are adding further pressure.
Some producers are using export restrictions to capture more value in domestic manufacturing, aiming to move beyond the role of sole mineral providers. Indonesia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Zimbabwe have introduced bans or limited exports of raw ores and concentrates, such as nickel, cobalt and lithium, to push processing at home. In Latin America, many governments have stepped up state control and licensing requirements. China, while controlling some important critical minerals, is also the leading refiner of most CRMs; its control of the value chain, as well as the limits it has applied to exports of rare earths and magnets, have created broad concerns about its dominant role in the overall production process of green and digital industries.
In light of the recent rise in CRM export restrictions, major consumers are de-risking their supply chains and coordinating with one another. The EU is pooling investment and purchasing, coordinating stockpiling and proposing limits on scrap exports; Australia is building a strategic reserve of critical minerals; India is offering incentives for rare earth magnet manufacturing; and G7 partners have launched a Critical Minerals Production Alliance. For some buyers, the urgency is immediate: a Japanese official told the Financial Times in October 2026 that Japan had “months, not years” of yttrium, a rare earth used in cars and chip manufacturing, left.
Partly in response to these frictions, CRM cooperation has become a key part of trade diplomacy: in just 21 months, 79 countries and blocs signed 139 agreements linked to critical minerals, from dedicated minerals deals to broad trade agreements that include CRM related provisions.
A global minerals race with a leader – and some strong contenders
The United States leads by a wide margin: 41 of its 48 mapped agreements (85%) are either exclusively centred (24) on CRMs or have strong CRM provisions (Figure 1). Many US CRM agreements follow a near-identical playbook for securing supply of outputs from mining and processing, and the emerging model of agreements on reciprocal trade (ARTs) now pursues CRM provisions as part of tariff deals. These agreements open partners’ mining and processing to US investment and coordinate finance, offtake, stockpiles and pricing, with some supporting local processing. They treat minerals as a national security and technology problem rather than a climate change-related issue, and in this context, efforts to decouple from China are playing a central role. Critical minerals is one of the few topics on which the current US administration is showing a global leadership ambition: in February 2026 the Office of the US Trade Representative launched a public consultation on the possible plurilateral Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals. The US and the EU together announced the Action Plan for Critical Minerals Supply Chain Resilience on 24 April 2026, following similar announcements with Mexico and Japan earlier in the year, which together could lay the building blocks for a possible plurilateral agreement.
Mineral diplomacy is not a US-only priority. Since 2025, India has signed 15 CRM-related agreements, China, Canada, Saudi Arabia, and the EU 11 each, and the UAE and Japan 10 each. Some jurisdictions, such as the EU, France, the DRC and Saudi Arabia, added critical minerals-related provisions to almost all agreements signed over the reviewed period.
Approaches differ. Canada and Saudi Arabia mostly sign dedicated CRM deals – such memoranda of understanding (MoUs) or joint declarations of intent. The EU, Japan, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) more often fold minerals into broader agreements, from free trade agreements (EU) and comprehensive economic partnership agreements (UAE) to cooperation frameworks (Japan, South Korea). China is among the most active economic agreement negotiators; however, only 11 of its 38 mapped agreements are CRM-linked, and these mostly with mineral-resource-rich countries. Its agreements are more often focused on energy cooperation, particularly centering on renewable energy priorities such as solar, wind and electric vehicles.
Who signs with whom: producers, consumers and hubs
Mineral diplomacy created a complex web of agreements: 79 countries and blocs are building partnerships. The United States casts the widest net, with 32 partners; for 8 of them, from Colombia to the Philippines, the US deal is their only CRM-linked agreement. Other consumer economies, such as India (14 partners), the EU (11) and South Korea (9), are building their own networks. Many of these agreements (94) include provisions focused on securing the necessary mineral supply. Japan (6 partners) has worked mainly through multiple agreements with other importers (the United States, the EU, and India), pointing to supply coordination among buyers.
Resource-rich countries are hubs in their own right. Indonesia had 12 CRM-linked partners, Argentina 10, Brazil 9 and Chile 7, though some of these partners come from bloc agreements. Many of the agreements (84) signed by such governments contained provisions aimed to build up stronger manufacturing downstream in producer countries, from scaling up exploration to local processing and skill-building. Gulf states act as investors and conveners: Saudi Arabia signed most of its minerals deals at its Future Minerals Forum, with producers such as Brazil, Chile and Zambia and buyers such as Canada, France and the United Kingdom, while the UAE builds minerals into economic partnership agreements with resource-rich countries.
There are also important producer-to-producer ties: Argentina, Bolivia, Chile and Peru signed a joint declaration on strategic minerals in August 2026, and the DRC has deals with Rwanda and Tanzania, pointing to scope for regional value chains. Producing countries are also using these deals to advance their own industrial goals, with provisions on building value chains at home now almost as common as those on buyers’ supply security.
The MoU moment: practical, fast, non-binding
Of the 139 CRM-linked agreements, 95 (68%) are MoUs, cooperation frameworks, joint statements or other non-binding instruments rather than more traditional legally-binding trade agreements such as free trade agreements (FTAs).
The appeal of this new MoU-diplomacy is speed. FTAs can take years to negotiate as their scope spans multiple sectors from agriculture to financial services. An MoU can be agreed in months, avoid parliamentary scrutiny and the necessity of ratification, and focus on a few issues that matter most to each side, whether it’s securing supply for importers or helping exporters develop production downstream in the value chain. MoUs also signal intent to investors and can pave the way for deeper agreements later.
MoUs might be weaker on follow-through. They are not legally binding, and their delivery rests on implementation arrangements that may not be immediately clear.
Many also lack transparency: 39% of CRM-related agreements’ texts are not published, so a significant part of CRM cooperation remains veiled, making it challenging to verify if the agreement’s objectives have been delivered upon.
Critical minerals and the climate agenda
While much critical mineral diplomacy is likely pursued with both climate and digital transition in mind, the climate agenda is rarely explicitly mentioned. Of all the 60 CRM-centred agreements, only 1 include additional energy provisions, 8 address heavy industry-related cooperation objectives, and none talk about broader climate governance. articles.title: China Moves to Strengthen Grip on Global Critical Mineral Market, Sparking National Security Concerns - The Washington Stand
articles.summary: China Moves to Strengthen Grip on Global Critical Mineral Market, Sparking National Security Concerns  The Washington Stand
articles.full_text:
China is moving to further expand its dominant global stranglehold on critical minerals that are vital to the manufacture of batteries, jet engines, semiconductors, and more, according to a new report. Experts say that the U.S. must leverage its global spending power to obtain a greater share in the minerals market, thereby enhancing national security.
On Wednesday, CNBC reported that Xi Jinping’s communist regime “is mobilizing state-linked companies to take bigger ownership stakes” in overseas mines that produce critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper, and more. Analysts say that the move would “give Beijing greater leverage over global supplies of critical minerals and who gets access to them.”
China is executing the plan by establishing a dedicated overseas bureau that will “oversee investments abroad by central state-owned enterprises.” According to analysts like Dan Wang, who serves as China director at Eurasia, this centralization push “could curb disorderly competition among Chinese firms and strengthen their hand against Western competitors and newer entrants, such as Saudi Arabia and India.”
Unlike Western nations, who have avoided investing in countries with rich mineral resources like Tajikistan and the Democratic Republic of Congo due to human rights concerns, Beijing has invested heavily in the two countries. According to a report from the Rhodium Group, the communist regime’s global mineral acquisitions reached $8.8 billion in the first three quarters this year — “already the highest annual total since at least 2018.”
Minerals such as lithium, cobalt, graphite, nickel, and others have become critical components of producing the technology that the world depends on, principally to manufacture rechargeable batteries that all phones, tablets, laptops, and other consumer electronic devices depend on. In addition, rare earth elements such as neodymium, yttrium, and samarium are critical to producing military equipment such as fighter jet motors, precision-guided munitions, and radar systems.
What has become increasing distressing to national security experts is that China, the U.S.’s number one adversary, has all but cornered the market on these critical minerals and rare earth elements. Beijing dominates the global mineral processing market (ranging from 40 to over 90% depending on the mineral) as well as the rare earth mining market at almost 70%. But in order to obtain the rare earth elements, the earth must be processed in refineries, of which Beijing produces 92% of due to taking on the high environmental costs that Western countries are unwilling to take on. As noted by CNBC, “The U.S. has abundant supplies of rare earths, but it relies on China to refine them.”
According to a report from The Wall Street Journal last month, the Trump administration has responded to the issue by attempting to create a China-free supply chain of minerals by directing hundreds of millions of dollars into domestic mineral projects as well as negotiating numerous bilateral agreements with countries in South America and Asia to import minerals. Data shows that the effort is slowly beginning to work, and U.S. officials say they are on track to remove China from the supply chain of some minerals within the next six to 12 months, while other minerals would take until 2030 to be China-free.
Still, experts like Gordon Chang, an author and distinguished senior fellow at the Gatestone Institute, say that while the Trump administration has made some progress in improving the U.S.’s market share of critical minerals, there is still much room for improvement.
“We can gear up on making ourselves resilient — something we’re doing already thanks to President Trump — but in the meantime we can use our superior bargaining position to force China to relax its de facto embargo,” he told The Washington Stand. “Trump, playing his strong hand weakly, has not wielded American power at his disposal.”
“At the moment, Xi Jinping has put his future in our hands by turning his back on his internal economy,” Chang added. “This means his only hope to rescue his economy, and his political system, is to export more. There is no replacement for the American market: We Americans account for about a third of global consumer spending. Trump, therefore, can use access to our market as a club. He botched the tariff campaign and has not used the threat of other tools that can keep Chinese products out.”

articles.title: ISMA Plugs Potential For 32 lakh jobs and USD 89 billion investment by 2047 In Solar Manufacturing - Saur Energy
articles.summary: ISMA Plugs Potential For 32 lakh jobs and USD 89 billion investment by 2047 In Solar Manufacturing  Saur Energy
articles.full_text:
India could transform its solar manufacturing industry into a fully integrated global powerhouse by 2047, creating 32.3 lakh direct and indirect jobs, attracting USD 89 billion in manufacturing investments and eliminating its solar import bill, according to a new report by the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA).
Titled Vision 2047: Solar Manufacturing from Polysilicon to Power Plant, the report presents a pathway for India to move beyond module assembly and establish manufacturing capabilities across the entire solar value chain—from polysilicon and ingots to wafers, cells and modules. The transition could enable India to retain a significantly larger share of the value generated by every solar panel manufactured domestically while strengthening its position in global markets.
Under the Vision 2047 pathway, India’s installed solar capacity could reach 2,275 GW by 2047, supported by manufacturing capacities of 3,266 GW in modules, 2,796 GW in cells, 2,479 GW in ingots and wafers, and 2,156 GW equivalent in polysilicon. The report estimates that the entire manufacturing chain could meet domestic demand within the next decade, with every stage progressively scaling up to support India’s growing solar installations and exports.
The expansion could create a significant employment opportunity, with total manufacturing-related jobs rising from approximately 4.1 lakh currently to 8.1 lakh by 2030 and 32.3 lakh by 2047. Direct employment within solar PV manufacturing plants could increase from around 1.4 lakh to 11.1 lakh. Notably, nearly 68% of direct manufacturing jobs could be concentrated in upstream segments such as cells, wafers and polysilicon by 2047, reflecting the growing importance of deeper domestic manufacturing capabilities.
The report estimates that approximately USD 89 billion in new solar PV manufacturing investments could be required by 2047 under the Vision pathway, translating into an average investment requirement of around USD 4.3 billion annually between 2027 and 2047. Nearly 70% of these investments are expected to flow into polysilicon, wafers and cells. The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme has already attracted approximately USD 8.4 billion in investments by June 2026, with every dollar of incentive drawing around four dollars in private investment.
A deeper domestic manufacturing ecosystem could also substantially reduce India’s dependence on imported solar components. The report projects that the country’s annual solar import bill could decline from approximately USD 4.4 billion currently to zero by 2041 under the Vision 2047 pathway. India could further account for 26.5% of global solar module supply by 2047, compared with around 5.9% under the current policy scenario by 2030.
Amit Manohar, Secretary General, ISMA, said, “India’s solar manufacturing sector stands at a pivotal moment, with the Vision 2047 pathway presenting an unprecedented opportunity to build a globally competitive, integrated manufacturing ecosystem. The potential to attract USD 89 billion in investments, generate over 32 lakh jobs and significantly reduce import dependence underscores the strategic importance of strengthening domestic manufacturing across the entire solar value chain. Realising this ambition will require sustained policy support, a predictable demand pipeline, investments in upstream manufacturing and continued efforts to strengthen India’s global competitiveness.”
The report identifies policy certainty, sustained domestic demand and timely implementation of manufacturing programmes as critical to realising this ambition. It calls for maintaining firm timelines under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), completing PLI-supported projects, expanding rooftop solar and agricultural solarisation programmes, and accelerating investments in upstream manufacturing. 
The Vision 2047 pathway outlines a phased transition, with cells scaling up through 2030, wafer manufacturing expanding through 2035 and the complete solar manufacturing value chain becoming established thereafter. This could position India not merely as a major solar deployment market, but as a trusted global supplier of solar manufacturing products and technologies.
In our view, ISMA’s vision of 32 lakh jobs and $89 billion in investment by 2047 is ambitious, but risks conflating manufacturing capacity with economic opportunity. The projections assume sustained policy support, predictable demand and globally competitive production, none of which is guaranteed. India’s experience with solar module overcapacity suggests that capacity additions can outpace demand, compress margins and weaken investment returns. Automation and scale could also limit job creation, particularly in upstream manufacturing. Moreover, eliminating imports does not automatically ensure cost competitiveness. The real test is whether India can build a viable, export-oriented manufacturing ecosystem without perpetual policy protection, rather than simply replicate China’s scale.

Introduction
Critical Copper Mining Corp. (CN:CCCU) is a junior mining company whose shares trade on the Canadian Securities Exchange. The name points toward copper, a metal that features heavily in discussions about electrification and critical minerals supply.

Recent Share Price Performance and Trading Volatility
The latest session ended with a fall of 72.22%, putting the quoted price at 0.05 CAD. Working backwards, that implies the shares were near 0.18 CAD before the slide.
The 260.00% volatility reading indicates that the trading range within the day was far wider than the closing price alone suggests. Such a spread usually appears when only a few orders set the price at any moment.
A tiny share price magnifies everything. Moving from 0.18 CAD to 0.05 CAD amounts to just thirteen cents, yet it translates into a loss of almost three quarters of the quoted value.
One session of this kind should not be read as a trend by itself. Sharp reversals frequently follow in either direction once the first wave of orders has cleared.
What Is Driving Critical Copper Mining's Stock Price Volatility?
Several forces tend to shape prices for small copper-oriented explorers. Financing terms come first, since a Placement priced well below the market can reset expectations overnight.
Metal prices add a second layer. Copper benchmarks, forecasts for electric vehicles and grid spending, and talk of Supply gaps all influence how much appetite exists for early-stage projects.
Corporate news matters just as much. A property acquisition, a field program, a change in management or a delay in a filing can each prompt a rapid repricing in a stock with few participants.
Finally, Liquidity itself acts as a driver. When bids are sparse, a single large sell order can push the quote down many ticks before another buyer appears.
Company Business Model and Fundamental Position
Companies of this type usually do not generate sales. They spend money on claims, geological work and administration, and they hope that results will eventually justify bigger programs or a sale of the asset.
For that reason, the Balance Sheet is more informative than any Earnings line. Cash on hand, the size of near-term commitments and the pace of share issuance determine how long fieldwork can continue.
Critical Copper Mining has issued relatively few announcements that are easy to find, so the details of its project portfolio, work plans and treasury are best checked directly in the company's own disclosures.
Readers should treat the copper theme in the corporate name as a descriptor of intent rather than as evidence of a defined deposit. Many copper juniors hold only early-stage ground, and the leap from claims to a producing mine is long, costly and uncertain.
Trading Volume, Liquidity, and Market Sentiment
Liquidity is the central issue for any stock at 0.05 CAD. A modest number of shares can move the price by several ticks, and exits can be difficult when sellers outnumber buyers.
Attitudes toward the company are likely to track the wider mood for copper and critical minerals explorers, as well as perceptions about how new Capital might be raised.
A quiet period without announcements can leave a stock drifting, whereas a clear update on work plans can draw in short-term traders quickly. That cuts both ways, because attention that arrives fast can leave just as fast.
Sustained recovery generally needs consistent participation over many sessions rather than one active day.

Exploration-stage companies face technical risk, since sampling and drilling may deliver little of economic interest. They also face financing risk, because they depend on outside capital to continue.
Price risk is heightened here. At 0.05 CAD, a few ticks can represent a double-digit percentage move, and rapid losses are possible.
Information risk deserves attention too. When public updates are infrequent, readers should rely on the company's own filings and disclosures and read them carefully.
What Investors Should Watch Next
The first item is any new company announcement, particularly one that describes projects, budgets or financing terms.
Next comes the trading pattern in the sessions that follow. Stabilization at a steady level, with moderate volume, would look different from another rapid slide.
Copper price direction and the general appetite for junior mining names will also frame the backdrop. Clear communication and measured share issuance would help rebuild confidence, whereas silence could keep the price unsettled.

Abstract
Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies1, but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale2,3,4,5,6. This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction4,5,6. Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Hydrogen (H) and hydrogen-containing compounds such as ammonia offer promising routes for low-carbon energy storage and utilization, supporting global decarbonization efforts1. Developing hydrogen energy technologies requires a fundamental understanding of how hydrogen interacts with materials. Hydrogen embrittles high-strength alloys in transport and storage systems2,7,8; its behaviour in metals determines the capacity and reversibility of solid-state storage9; hydride formation in zirconium-alloy cladding threatens fission reactor integrity10; and isotope retention is critical to fusion viability11. Across all of these applications, knowing where hydrogen resides in materials is essential.
Hydrogen in crystalline materials exists in three principal states: dissolved as an interstitial solute in solid solution8, bonded to hydrogen-affinitive elements as thermodynamically stable hydrides (for example, titanium hydride)12,13 or trapped at crystal defects, including vacancies14,15, dislocations3,16 and grain boundaries3,17. Experimentally, these states can be analysed by APT2,4, which uses time-of-flight mass spectrometry to identify hydrogen with nanoscale spatial resolution. In practice, deuterium (2H or D) is often introduced instead of protium to distinguish genuine hydrogen signals from background hydrogen in the instrument, which is predominantly 1H (refs. 4,5).
Among the three states, hydrides and defect-trapped hydrogen have been investigated more extensively by APT. Hydrides are identifiable through their characteristic stoichiometries12,13 and defect-trapped hydrogen can often be co-localized with solute-decorated defects (for example, Cottrell atmospheres such as that of carbon)3,16. When defects are not decorated with identifiable elements, associating hydrogen with defect traps becomes challenging because such defects are ‘invisible’ in APT, unless correlative techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are used16,18.
By contrast, characterizing hydrogen in solid solutions is particularly challenging for several reasons. First, the solubility of hydrogen is generally low in many alloys; for example, body-centred cubic (BCC) iron typically contains only a few tens of atomic parts per million (at. ppm) of hydrogen2,7,8, which approaches the APT detection limit6,19. Second, unlike hydrogen in stable hydrides, interstitial hydrogen is highly mobile and can diffuse to the surface and desorb before analysis20,21; cryogenic sample transfer (cryo-transfer) for APT mitigates, but does not eliminate, such signal loss4,20,22.
A further complication arises from the methods used to introduce hydrogen into the needle-shaped APT specimens. Electrochemical charging is commonly used2,4, but it can impose extremely high hydrogen fugacity on the specimen and generate large numbers of vacancies—so-called ‘superabundant vacancies’14,23. Further artefacts can be introduced during specimen preparation: electron-beam or ion-beam irradiation in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) or focused ion beam (FIB) can also create vacancies that subsequently trap hydrogen15. Careful interpretation of APT hydrogen maps is therefore required whenever SEM-FIB processing has been used.
In this study, we use a series of FCC alloys as model systems to address this challenge. Compared with BCC alloys, FCC lattices offer higher hydrogen solubility and lower diffusivity7,24, improving signal-to-noise ratio and reducing diffusion-related losses. Our results provide experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in FCC metallic solid solutions and establish a methodological basis for robust, artefact-aware APT characterization of hydrogen in materials.
Deuterium in precipitate-free FCC MPEA lattice
Throughout this study, APT tip specimens were electrolytically charged with deuterium, which saturates specimens more efficiently than gaseous charging, while reducing corrosion concerns3,4. Voltage pulsing rather than laser pulsing was used for all APT analyses to minimize ambiguity in deuterium signal identification against instrumental background hydrogen4,6. This alloy is known to have a locally distorted lattice, which can more effectively hinder hydrogen diffusion and thus reduce signal loss26.
Immediately after D charging, we spent approximately 3 s to remove the D-charging electrolyte and then quenched the charged tips in liquid nitrogen (LN2) to ‘freeze’ the deuterium in the MPEA.
Once LN2 evaporation stopped—indicating thermal equilibration between the tips and LN2—the specimens were transferred into the APT system using the cryo-transfer procedure described previously3.

The H map shows a hydrogen-rich cap at the specimen apex, which arises from the field-induced migration and evaporation of ambient hydrogen adsorbed on the tip surface during APT analysis4.
By contrast, the D map shows a relatively homogeneous and random distribution, consistent with what is expected for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution.

Because deuterium can segregate to defects that are not visible in APT (ref. 16), we carefully evaluated whether the observed deuterium distribution is truly random. We performed nearest-neighbour analyses of deuterium atoms, as shown in Fig. 1c,d, for the first and fifth nearest deuterium neighbours, respectively. This approach detects clustering by comparing interatomic distances between deuterium atoms in the experimental dataset with those in a randomized dataset of equivalent size19,27. A marked shift towards shorter distances indicates clustering, whereas agreement with the random distribution is consistent with deuterium occupying a large population of equivalent interstitial sites27.
Figure 1c shows the distribution of deuterium–deuterium pair distances for the first nearest neighbour. The most probable pair distance in the experimental data is close to that in the randomized dataset (both approximately 0.8 nm), indicating that the deuterium atoms are randomly distributed. We repeated the analysis for the fifth nearest deuterium neighbour (Fig. 1d) and obtained a consistent result, with a larger most probable distance of about 1.2 nm, as expected when a more distant neighbour is considered. These results are consistent with interstitial deuterium (as a proxy of hydrogen) in solid solution. Figure 1 therefore suggests the effectiveness of cryo-APT for preserving the charged D atoms and enabling observation of their distribution in solid solution. Canada’s drive to reduce its dependence on American energy markets and establish itself as a global LNG supplier is attracting serious institutional capital.
A consortium led by Blackstone (NYSE: BX) has agreed to acquire 49.9% of the LNG Canada stake held by a Mitsubishi Corporation unit, with the total transaction valued at $3.1 billion.
Four major Canadian pension and investment funds are co-investing alongside Blackstone (NYSE: BX): the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System, the Investment Management Corp. of Ontario, and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board.
Despite the stake sale, Mitsubishi Corporation will retain its position as controlling partner and preserve its full share of LNG offtake from the project.
LNG Canada, situated in Kitimat, British Columbia, is the country’s first LNG export facility and currently holds a production capacity of 14 million tonnes per annum.
The Phase 2 expansion, which received its final investment decision just weeks before this deal was announced, will add two processing trains and double total output capacity to 28 million tonnes per annum.
Commercial production from the expanded facility is not expected to begin until the early 2030s, making this a long-horizon infrastructure bet for the investors involved.
Shell, the world’s largest LNG trader, holds a 40% interest in LNG Canada and stands to receive nearly 6 million additional tonnes per annum of supply from the Phase 2 expansion.
The project carries significant political weight, having topped Prime Minister Mark Carney’s list of five major national priority projects designed to diversify Canadian energy exports away from the United States.
Blackstone’s Infrastructure and Asset Based Credit platform, which oversees roughly $140 billion and employs more than 100 investment professionals, has been deepening its footprint in Canadian assets through partnerships with domestic institutional investors.
The transaction underscores how sovereign-adjacent capital pools are increasingly gravitating toward large-scale energy infrastructure at a moment when energy security has become a central theme in Canadian economic policy.
With global LNG demand remaining robust and Canada eager to monetize its natural gas reserves through Pacific export routes, the Kitimat facility sits at the intersection of national strategy and institutional investment appetite.
